#6438. Planets Don't Just Disappear, But They Can Wobble Out of Sight if Their Neighbour is Close Enough

NASA's TESS mission was a success by almost any measure. So far, as of mid-October 2026, it's identified more than 8,100 candidate exoplanets, and just over 1,000 of them have been confirmed. The mission is still ongoing, and astronomers are also finding more exoplanets in its archival data with new machine learning techniques.

TESS was primarily aimed at finding smaller super-Earths and sub-Neptunes, but it also found many hot-Jupiters during its mission. One of them, about 1,000 light years away, is a hot Jupiter named TOI-2535b and it exhibited some strange behaviour. TESS observed multiple transits by TOI-2535b over seven years, then the planet seemed to just disappear.

Planets can't just disappear, unless the Death Star is nearby, and astronomers have wondered what's behind the hot Jupiter's disappearing act. New research in The Astrophysical Journal Letters has a natural explanation for the vanished star. It's titled "A TESS Disappearing Act: The Vanishing Transits of TOI-2535 b," and the corresponding author is Samuel Yee, a postdoctoral fellow at UCLA.

"Planetary transits require a fortuitous alignment between a planetâs orbit and our line of sight, but dynamical interactions can render this geometric coincidence only temporary," the authors write in their research letter. "We report the discovery of the hot Jupiter TOI-2535b, the first confirmed planet orbiting a single star whose transits have been directly observed to disappear."

Detecting planets via the transit method only works if everything lines up, as the authors explain. But everything doesn't necessarily stay lined up. Dynamical interactions abound in solar systems, as we know from our own Solar System's history. Giant planets have migrated, ending old, stable orbital patterns and heralding new ones. Interactions can scatter smaller objects, and even send comets careening into the inner Solar System.

But a massive shift isn't required to upset the finely-tuned line of sight that allows us to see distant exoplanets as they transit their stars.

"Because a planet is only observed to transit when its orbit normal is within a few degrees of the sky plane, even small changes in a planetâs orbital inclination can result in measurable changes in its transit shape," the authors explain. "For sufficiently large inclination changes, a planet may only have the correct transit geometry for a fraction of its dynamical evolution."

Here's the kicker: "If the variation is fast enough and we are lucky to catch the planet in the right phase of its inclination evolution, we may see its transits appear or disappear," the researchers write.

This figure presents some of the research's findings. The first panel shows TESS transits from sectors 10, 63, and 90. Sectors are rectangular strips of the sky that TESS observes. The second panel shows the movement of the transit chord across the stellar disk. The dark circle shows TOI-2535b's size relative to its star. Image Credit: Samuel W. Yee et al 2026 ApJL 1011 L60

That's what happened with TOI-2535b, according to this work, and it's probably because of another exoplanet interacting with the hot Jupiter.

By watching it over several years, astronomers observed TOI-2535b's orbit in detail. It didn't just suddenly disappear. Both the timing and the shape of the transit slowly changed.

This can happen with circumbinary exoplanets, those that orbit a binary star. "Circumbinary planets frequently exhibit rapid changes in their transit impact parameters," the authors write. "As a result, even a small misalignment between the two orbits leads to intervals when the planet may transit both, one, or neither of its host stars."

But TOI-2535b orbits a single star, making its disappearance extremely unusual. "Around single stars, inclination variations of planets are typically less dramatic and appear to be relatively rare," the researchers explain. But that's what seems to be happening here due to the influence of another exoplanet.

âWe think of the universe as resembling clockwork, where everything is regular, but thatâs not true. If there are multiple planets in a system, they can affect each otherâs orbits. We know of a few systems that are like this,â said Yee. âThis is the most extreme example weâve seen because the two planets are interacting so strongly. The planetâs orbit is tilting so quickly that its transit disappeared while we were watching.â

This work rests partly on what are called Transit Duration Variations (TDV). These are small yet measurable and periodic changes in the amount of time it takes for an exoplanet to complete a transit in front of its star. TOI-2535b's TDVs are unusual, according to the authors, and so are the changes in its orbital inclination.

"The TOI-2535 system is an unusual and exceptional system in many ways. Observationally, it has the largest TDVs and inclination change ever observed for a planet orbiting a single star, with a precession period of decades, shorter than other known systems," the authors explain. The system also has some of the largest Transit Timing Variations (TTVs) ever detected, and they're definitely the largest ever detected for a hot Jupiter.

The researchers say that another, neighbouring exoplanet of Saturn-mass or greater is tugging on the exoplanet's orbit, making it "disappear." This is surprising, since hot Jupiter's aren't expected to have any close neighbours. In the rare cases where they do have neighbours, the neighbours are quite a bit less massive.

"This makes TOI-2535b one of only a handful of hot Jupiters known to have a close-by planetary companion. Furthermore, the companion to TOI-2535b is likely a second short-period giant planet. This differs from all but one of the currently known hot Jupiters with a nearby companion, in which the companions are sub-Neptunes or super-Earths," the authors write.

A pair of massive gas giants orbiting one system in resonance with each other isn't something planet-formation models predict. The authors rule out high-eccentricity migration as a cause. "Such systems could not have formed through high-eccentricity migration, which has been posited to be responsible for most other hot Jupiters," the authors write. But there are two other migration possibilities.

In one, the planet is pulled into an eccentric orbit by a powerful interaction of some sort, possibly a near collision with another object, and then the star's gravity pulls it in, where it takes up residence as a hot Jupiter.

The second scenario sees the planet pulled into the inner solar system with other planets inside the protoplanetary disk. But that counterindicates the observed orbital tilts. "However, the protoplanetary disk would also quickly damp the inclinations of the two planets, requiring some later excitation to explain the nonzero inclination required by the TDVs," the authors write.

An illustration of a protoplanetary disk. It's possible that the planet was pulled into the inner system with other planets inside the protoplanetary disk. But disks tend to flatten orbital inclinations. So something else would've had to happen to explain the exoplanet inclinations. Image Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/T. Pyle (SSC) - February, 2005

There are other possibilities, but they're outliers that "only operate in specific regions of the space of possible planetary orbital parameters," and only an accurate understanding of the system's overall architecture could confirm any of them. The researchers don't have that yet.

These are the types of solar system architectures that intrigue astronomers because they hint at new processes. Somehow, components of the system have interacted in ways that have produced a very unusual situation: a pair of massive planets close to their star. Not only that, but we can watch their interactions play out over only a few years, which is very rare.

"Our dynamical modeling reveals that the perturber is likely of Saturn-mass or greater and in a mean-motion resonance with TOI-2535b, making this an unusual system that contains two short-period giant planets," the authors write. "The TDVs measured for TOI-2535b represent one of the most extreme examples of planetâplanet interactions driving orbital evolution on human timescales."

If there were only a single close-in planet, a more ready explanation would offer itself. But because there's a pair, the researchers have to reach further for an explanation.

âBecause TOI-2535 b has a close neighbor, it probably migrated by slowly spiraling in instead of getting flung in,â Yee said. âWe may be seeing a formation channel that doesnât happen very often but is very interesting.â

#6437. The Best Espresso Machines for Every Budget, Tested and Approved by a Barista

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Few things make a workday better than a delicious espresso drink, especially one made in the convenience of your own home. They’re more potent than your standard cup of coffee and require a bit more know-how, but the payoff is worth it.

Once you dip your toe into the world of espresso makers, you might find yourself overwhelmed by the dizzying array of options. Stovetop espresso makers, manual espresso machines, Nespresso, and fully automatic — there are many appliances to choose from.

To determine which is right for you, it’s helpful to start with the basics. We spoke with Stephen Welch, who has over nine years of experience in the coffee industry and serves as the coffee development manager for Pret A Manger USA. Welch is also a certified Q Grader, which is akin to becoming a sommelier in the coffee world.

To recommend the espresso machines below, we combined our own testing with thorough research. We brewed espresso with some models on this list for three months, and considered our previous experience with capsule machines and stovetop makers. Reviews from expert sites, including Good Housekeeping and coffee specialty sites like Coffee Geek, also informed our selections. We also consulted Sarah Connor, Popular Mechanics Reviews Editor and former barista, who recently did hands-on testing with two different machines in our office.

For each model, we evaluated its type, price, durability, and features, such as a built-in descaling alert, so you know when to perform a deep clean on your machine. Our list of the 10 best espresso machines includes a variety of options at different price points and for all levels of coffee-making experience.

Earlier this year, we tested this machine hands-on against a comparable De'Longhi model, and the coffee from this machine came out on top. The Breville Barista Express Impress  features an integrated conical-burr grinder with 25 grind settings, feeding directly into its impress system, which handles dosing and tamping with an assisted tamp that applies about 10kg of pressure and finishes with a 7-degree “barista twist.”

The thermo-coil heating system ensures highly accurate brew temperatures and consistent extraction. With a 250-gram bean hopper and 2-liter water reservoir, plus full stainless construction and a manual micro-foam steam wand for milk-based drinks, it delivers café-style performance in a compact home footprint.

Like a great prosumer digital camera, the Barista Express has all the capabilities and controls of a manual, pro-level espresso maker, but in a convenient package that allows even first-timers to pull a near-perfect shot. It's included grinder has controls for the amount and size of the grind, and the espresso machine gives you full control over the length of the pour. The single-boiler maker heats up in three seconds, and pulling a shot takes less than 20 seconds from grind to that first sip of frothy crema. After months of testing several machines, this one offers the most capabilities, most consistent pours, in the most user-friendly package that everyone from new enthusiasts to third-wave fanatics will appreciate.

Similar in price and capabilities to the Barista Pro, De’Longhi’s La Specialista Prestigio offers a few additional features that some espresso lovers might prefer. To take the stress out of tamping, De’Longhi has equipped this machine with a lever on the side, which you can pull to tamp your beans before removing them from the built-in grinder. That saves time, eliminates spilled grinds, and provides an even tamp. It’s the most convenient system we’ve tested, but you do lose some precision in the process, which might bother some purists.

The machine offers three heat settings for more control, however, a feature that the Barista Pro does not. It also has a secondary heating system, enabling you to move from pouring shots to steaming milk in seconds. It’s an excellent semi-automatic machine that trades some control for extra convenience while still delivering tasty shots with frothy crema.

This machine from KitchenAid delivers a professional-grade brew in a home environment. With a 2.2-liter removable water tank and durable metal-clad housing, it integrates a built-in bean hopper and grinder featuring “smart dosing” for consistent extraction. The single-spout delivery system supports 15 preset recipes (espresso, latte, Americano, etc.), and the automatic milk frother draws from a milk hose to one-touch froth and heat.

Simple, compact and affordable, the ECP36300 is capable of producing nice-tasting shots of espresso and frothy steamed milk without much fuss. The stainless steel boiler is durable, but takes longer to heat up than more expensive units. And because there’s just one heating element, you’ll need to budget even more time to fire up the steaming wand to froth your milk. The included tamper is made of flimsy plastic that can pack your grind unevenly; we suggest buying one made of metal for better results. You’ll also need your own grinder for this machine. But as long as you can summon some extra patience in the morning (a hard task, we know), this machine is great value and a good option for anyone with limited counter space.

This semi-automatic espresso maker isn’t cheap, but because it’s a KitchenAid, you know it’s extremely durable. If you’ve got a house full of regular coffee drinkers, we recommend you go with something like a KitchenAid that can stand up to heavy use. This one comes with a lot of nice features, too, like a cup warmer on top and a milk frothing attachment (sold separately). The milk frother also gets high marks from reviewers.

If you’ve got a limited budget, consider this classic stovetop espresso maker. It looks sleek on the countertop and makes a great cup of espresso without the extra cost of a larger machine. It’s not as easy to use as a fully automated machine, and it requires cleaning after each use. Because there’s no programming in the machine, it also won’t remind you about regular descaling.

The Flair allows you to customize everything about your espresso-making experience, including the water pressure, the water-to-coffee ratio, and the amount of crema or espresso foam on top. If you’re a true coffee geek, this is absolutely the machine for you. And it looks pretty darn cool, too.

At one point in my life, there was nothing more horrifying than the idea of making coffee from a single-use capsule. But after a few stays at hotels with in-room capsule espresso machines, I had to admit that the resulting espresso isn’t just good enough but actually pretty darn great. The Vertuo Next has a more plastic look than I’d like in a machine, but there is no denying how simple and dependable it is. And in terms of the environmental impact, it’s actually not as bad as you might think, particularly if you’re recycling the capsules.—J.S.

The Maestro is a beautiful machine. Of course, it should be for $1,300. But you do get a lot for the price, as you can customize just about everything such as the grind of the bean, the strength or “dose” of the coffee, and the particular type of espresso drink including a cappuccino or a flat white.

An espresso refers to how you prepare a drink rather than the type of coffee bean you use or its roast. Essentially, espresso is concentrated coffee “generally prepared quickly under pressure,” Welch says. The process involves pulling water through the cake, or bed, of packed ground coffee to extract a shot of coffee into your glass.

Water temperature and pressure are critical. According to a Smithsonian article about the history of espresso machines, Italian coffee chain Illy specifies water should be between 190 to 200 degrees Fahrenheit and under 9 atmospheres of pressure or more. These amounts vary slightly depending on equipment and the barista’s preference.

The difference between manual and automatic espresso machines also comes down to technique. Machines that “require physical force to press the water through the bed” of coffee are classified as manual, Welch says. Generally, you pull a lever, but some portable machines operate via a button or press. Manual extraction allows you to vary the pressure as you extract, which many home espresso enthusiasts want to control themselves to achieve their perfect drink. Keep in mind that manual espresso makers can have automated features.

All automatic machines use an “electrical component to activate the pump to push the water through the coffee bed,” Welch says. Automating the extraction process allows you to achieve a more consistent beverage. Although you give up a degree of control and customization, you gain a consistently dependent beverage. There are different types of automated machines:

If you are a true espresso enthusiast and have the time and interest to craft espresso according to the traditional method at home, opt for a manual or semi-automatic machine. If you want a traditionally-brewed espresso without having to prepare it yourself, consider a fully automatic machine.

Stovetop espresso makers and pod-style capsule machines also make concentrated coffee drinks, but aren’t technically espresso machines. In the case of stovetop makers, these appliances use steam pressure and don’t reach the requisite amount of water pressure. Most capsule machines add more water than a true espresso, producing something more akin to an Americano, Welch says. But you can make different specialty drinks depending on what type of pod you buy.

Despite these design differences, we chose to include stovetop and capsule machines on our list. They’re an affordable, convenient alternative to true espresso machines that can still produce a delicious, concentrated coffee drink despite the lack of manual control.

#6436. Scientists Discover a Strange Form of Iron on the Moon That Shouldn’t Be There

Scientists examining lunar soil collected by China’s Chang’e-6 mission have discovered an unexpected form of iron preserved within microscopic impact glass.

Tiny particles of iron trapped inside lunar glass may preserve evidence of the Moon’s ancient magnetic history. Scientists studying soil returned by China’s Chang’e-6 mission have identified face-centered cubic γ-Fe, an unusual form of metallic iron never before confirmed in natural lunar samples.

The discovery is particularly unexpected because γ-Fe normally exists only at high temperatures and changes into a different crystal structure as it cools. Yet researchers found that this phase of iron had survived inside microscopic glass particles formed during impacts on the lunar surface.

Researchers led by Prof. Haifeng Du of the High Magnetic Field Laboratory at the Hefei Institutes of Physical Science (HFIPS) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) examined impact glass containing numerous nanoscale iron particles. Using focused ion beam preparation, transmission electron microscopy, and chemical analysis, they confirmed that γ-Fe was the dominant iron phase in the two glass samples studied. Their findings were published September 16 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS).

Under normal conditions, γ-Fe transforms into α-Fe as temperatures fall. The team proposed that the extreme conditions created by lunar impacts could prevent this transformation. Rapid cooling of molten material, small amounts of carbon and other elements, and the surrounding glassy matrix may have helped preserve the unusual crystal structure at the lunar surface.

The scientists also investigated whether these particles could retain magnetic information. Using off-axis electron holography, a technique that can map magnetic fields at extremely small scales, they examined the magnetic structure of individual γ-Fe nanoparticles. Relatively large particles displayed a stable single-vortex magnetic state, with their magnetization arranged in a circulating pattern. They also maintained a stable magnetic response when exposed to an external magnetic field.

“This tiny magnetic fossil may help us better understand the Moon’s ancient magnetic history,” said Dr. Long Li of HFIPS, a member of the research team.

Although the Moon no longer possesses a global magnetic field, its rocks and soils contain magnetic minerals that can preserve information about past conditions. The newly identified γ-Fe expands the range of materials scientists can investigate when reconstructing that history.

Because γ-Fe and α-Fe develop under different physical conditions and exhibit distinct magnetic properties, they may retain records from different stages of lunar impact events. Further research will be needed to determine how reliably these minerals preserve ancient magnetic signals and what they can reveal about the evolution of magnetism on the Moon.

Reference: “Magnetic vortex state of natural lunar γ-Fe” by Pengfei Liu, Ziliang Jin, Zheng Gong, Long Li, Kang Wang, Xiandi Zeng, Jing Liu, Dongsheng Song, Haifeng Du, Kelei Zhu, Chuanxin Yan, Jinhua Li, Keke Zhang, Wyn Williams and Ann M. Hirt, 16 September 2026, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2608395123

#6435. The Chandra X-Ray Observatory Unmasks a Supernova Impostor

When is an apparent supernova not really a supernova at all? That's a tough question to answer, especially since no supernovae have been observed in the Milky Way in the telescope era. The ones that astronomers see are mostly many millions of light years away in distant galaxies.

SN 1987A was the closest modern supernova, but it exploded in the Large Magellanic Cloud, which is still more than 160,000 light years away. And that was before the Hubble launched, and studying its aftermath was difficult. Now we have automated supernova surveys that scan the sky for exploding stars. One such survey detected what seemed to be a supernovae in 2016, in a distant galaxy.

Sometimes, a star exhibits variations in brightness before it explodes as supernovae, and that can create confusion around what's actually happening. That describes the object detected in 2016.

That object was a massive star in a distant galaxy that's showing behaviour associated with a typical supernova explosion. Supernovae explosions are the final act of massive stars that reach the end of their lives, and their prodigious energy output can light up the sky. That's what this star does, sort of.

But unlike a supernova with a single explosion, this star has a volatile outburst every 113 days, something that no supernova can repeat. In an effort to understand what's behind these repeated outbursts, astronomers turned to one of NASA's workhorse space telescopes, the Chandra X-ray Observatory. Chandra's exceptional angular resolution sets it apart from other x-ray observatories, and it can pick out faint sources in detail at great distances.

The volatile star, named AT 2016blu, has about 33 solar masses and is in the spiral galaxy NGC 4559, around 30 million light years away. AT stands for astronomical transient, and blu is a sequential suffix that tells us the star was the 1,685th transient reported in the year 2016. AT 2016blu is also called a luminous blue variable (LBV), and was first discovered in 2012 by an automated supernova search.

LBVs are rare, and as noted above, exhibit powerful variations in both their brightness and their spectra. Their variability is usually considered to be unpredictable, but in this case, it's periodic.

New research in The Astrophysical Journal has an explanation for AT 2016blu. It's titled "AT 2016blu: Accretion-powered Outbursts in a Luminous Blue Variable and Compact Object Binary," and the lead author is Mojgan Aghakhanloo, a Virginia Institute of Theoretical Astronomy Origins Fellow at the University of Virginia in Charlottesville.

"We present the first X-ray detection of the supernova (SN) impostor AT 2016blu in NGC 4559," the authors write.

Astronomers are calling AT 2016blu a 'supernova impostor' because LBVs are often detected in supernova searches. "Supernova (SN) impostors are transient events associated with massive stars that are often initially discovered in SN surveys," the authors explain. "However, because their outbursts are less energetic and less luminous than true SNe, and because the star is expected to survive, they are subsequently classified as SN impostors."

Unlike a supernove, AT 2016blu appears to have a nearby companion that triggers the outbursts.

"AT 2016blu exhibited 27 detected quasiperiodic (â¼113 day) outbursts between 2012 and 2026 June, presumably triggered by periastron passages in an eccentric binary system in which the primary is a â³33 Mâ luminous blue variable (LBV)," the authors explain.

Chandra had observed AT 2016blu by accident in 2001-2002, but that was before its first documented outburst. Those observations were actually aimed at another nearby ultraluminous X-ray source (ULX), NGC 4559 X7. XMM-Newton, an ESA x-ray observatory, also observed AT 2016blu four times while looking at NGC 4559 X7. So there's a collection of happenstance observations of the region.

âFor 15 years, astronomers have been watching this star get really bright and then dim again on a regular basis,â said lead author Aghakhanloo. âUntil we were able to get Chandra data at the right time, we couldnât figure out what was making this happen.â

Overall, astronomers observed 27 outbursts of optical light from the supernova impostor between 2012 and 2026. That's one burst about every 113 days, something no supernova can do, since they're destroyed in their explosive outbursts.

âThis starâs behavior was confusing at first because it kept acting like a supernova, but clearly itâs not because it keeps surviving these outbursts about three times a year,â said co-author NÃºria Torres-AlbÃ , also of the University of Virginia. âTo understand the cause of these eruptions, we realized we needed X-ray data that was timed so that weâd observe the star when it was in an outburst.â

Once it was known to exhibit outbursts, the researchers watched it in optical light leading up to its next predicted outburst. Then they used Chandra to observe it in x-rays, since it's the only x-ray telescope powerful enough to discern AT 2016blu from the other nearby x-ray source, ULX NGC 4559 X7, which is much brighter than the supernova impostor. "We monitored the sourceâs visual-wavelength variability around its predicted outburst time and triggered a Chandra Target of Opportunity (ToO) program in 2026 March, obtaining observations with detections over five closely spaced epochs," the authors write.

The left panel shows a stacked Chandra image of all five target-of-opportunity observations taken during the 2026 March optical outburst of AT 2016blu, in a span of 4 days. The right panel is an XMM-Newton image of the same sky region. XMM-Newton is not as powerful as Chandra, and cannot resolve the two sources. The image is dominated by ULX NGC 4559 X7, much brighter than AT 2016blu. Image Credit: Mojgan Aghakhanloo et al 2026 ApJ 1011 252

âWe suspected that the bright repeating flashes at optical wavelengths might actually be powered by periodic blasts of high-energy X-rays,â said co-author Nathan Smith of the University of Arizona in Tucson. âThe dense gas surrounding the system is heated by the X-rays and then glows in the optical. So, we needed to plan the Chandra X-ray observations carefully to be simultaneous with an optical outburst.â

Chandra's x-ray data from its 2026 outburst shows that AT 2016blu is 100 times brighter in x-rays than in its data from 2001 to 2002. This is best explained by a binary companion. "These outbursts are most likely triggered by periastron encounters in an eccentric binary system in which the primary is an LBV," the authors write. The secondary is almost certainly a neutron star or a black hole. As they orbit each other, the LBV ejects material that finds its way to the secondary. The material orbits the secondary at very high speeds in an accretion ring, and that heats it up until it emits x-rays.

Based on the x-ray luminosity, the researchers estimate that about 2.7% of Earth's mass is transferred during each outburst.

As is often the case, the researchers had to rule out a potential background source, and for that they relied on Chandra, too. "The alternative to a genuine counterpart to AT 2016blu would be a background quasar with a coincident position," the researchers explain. "This quasar, furthermore, would have brightened at a time coincident with our observations, and thus the AT 2016blu outburst."

These panels are all Chandra images. The first five are from Chandra's observations of AT 2016blu during the ToO campaign, and it's clearly visible during its outbursts. The sixth panel is a stacked image of the region outside of an outburst, clearly showing no background quasar. "No source is detected in the stacked archival images prior to the first observed optical outburst of AT 2016blu, when it was a stable system," the researchers explain. Image Credit: Mojgan Aghakhanloo et al 2026 ApJ 1011 252

"AT 2016blu represents the first observationally known LBV system with a compact companion," the authors write. "Previously studied LBVs either lack X-ray detections or show luminosities consistent with windâwind collisions in massive-star binaries."

Its discovery could shed light on other, similar transient phenomena. Many stars show changes in brightness before they explode as supernovae, and maybe some of them are similar to AT 2016bu. "The discovery of an LBVâcompact-object binary undergoing accretion-powered outbursts also connects AT 2016blu to a growing class of models in which massive starâcompact object binaries explain a variety of pre-SN transient phenomena," the authors explain.

The next step, as is often the case in observations of new types of astrophysical objects, is to find more of them.

"Expanding the sample of such systems is therefore essential to better understand the evolutionary pathways and physical mechanisms connecting SN impostors, LBVs, and interacting SNe," the researchers conclude.

A new study points to testosterone and proteins in the skin as reasons why males and females experience temperatures differently.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's a common observation that women often prefer warmer temperatures and feel cold more easily than men do, and the same trend appears among females of other species. Now, a study offers new clues as to what drives this preference — and testosterone may play a part.

Skin carries sensors to detect heat and cold that influence each organism's decision to stay in or move out of an environment. The new study, published Oct. 28 in the Journal of Physiology, found that these sensors activate at higher temperatures in female mice, which appears to shift their preferred temperature roughly 7 degrees Fahrenheit (4 degrees Celsius) higher than that of male mice. Testosterone seems to influence this difference in activation.

"You could say it's just a cute observation of no particular importance," said study co-author Peter McNaughton, a pharmacologist at King's College London who studies pain, thermal sensation and thermoregulation. "[But] it's got practical ramifications," in that it might be important in designing buildings and spaces that accommodate people, he told Live Science.

Proteins in the skin's nerve endings activate in response to warmth or cold. "You can look at them like little electrical generators in the nerve endings," said Dr. Michael Caterina, a neuroscientist at Johns Hopkins University who was not involved in the research.

When activated, these proteins allow charged ions to enter sensory nerve cells, which, in turn, transmit electrical signals to the brain. The circuits a given nerve cell connects to determines our perception of heat or cold, Caterina told Live Science.

Beyond humans, it is known that many female animals, including mice and birds, prefer slightly warmer temperatures than their male counterparts do. So the researchers set up an experiment to investigate these differences.

They put 30 male and 27 female mice on two adjacent plates of different temperatures — one at 91.4 degrees Fahrenheit (33 degrees Celsius) and another that varied between lower and higher temperatures. A camera tracked the mice's movements and calculated how much time they spent on each plate.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Both male and female mice spent more time at the 91.4 F plate when the second plate was cooler. However, when put next to a plate measuring 100.4 F (38 C), female mice spent significantly more time on the warmer plate than male mice did. The average preferred surface temperature was approximately 89.6 F (32 C) for male mice and 96.8 F (36 C) for female mice.

"Since the top of the cage was completely open, there was no question of the air temperature affecting the mice," McNaughton said, so the preference was driven solely by the sensors in their skin. The researchers also measured the internal and skin temperatures of the mice and confirmed that there were no significant differences between the sexes on those fronts.

The scientists explored what would happen if they genetically deleted the warmth-detector protein. In male mice, this reduced their avoidance of the warmer plate, suggesting this protein normally sends a signal that discourages them from staying on warmer surfaces. The mice's preferred temperature also rose to about 95 F (35 C), closer to that of females.

The study suggests that testosterone somehow tweaks the function of heat-sensing nerves in the skin.

In female mice, deleting or blocking the protein did not have any significant effect.

The team then tried eliminating or blocking the coolness-detecting protein, finding that males and females didn't avoid the cool plates as strongly as they did before. Female mice also spent less time on the warmer plates, but males' preference for the warmer plates didn't change.

"Females are a little bit more responsive to activation of the cold receptor," Caterina said, "and a little bit less responsive to activation of the warmer receptor." That's despite the temperature-sensing neurons in both sets of mice working identically, the team found.

The researchers suspected that sex hormones might help to explain this difference.

They gave a group of male mice a drug that blocks the production of testosterone. Weeks after the treatment, these mice spent more time on the 38 C plate than males with normal testosterone. Meanwhile, female mice given testosterone lost their preference for warmer temperatures.

Interestingly, giving male mice female hormones, including forms of estrogen and progesterone, did not affect their temperature preferences. And blocking the hormones in female mice also had no effect. These hormones are known to influence other aspects of temperature regulation in the body, though, such as heat dissipation through the skin; but in this case, they didn't seem to affect animals' perception of temperature.

"So it really seems as though testosterone is the most important determinant," McNaughton said. But these changes were only partial; testosterone did not completely reverse the differences between the sexes. "So there is something else going on that we weren't able to identify," he added.

The exact mechanism for how testosterone impacts the sensor proteins is not clear. Because the effect happened over weeks, researchers suggested that it did not directly affect the temperature-sensing proteins. It might instead act indirectly by influencing the activity of genes, but further studies would be needed to confirm this idea.

Although the researchers did not conduct any tests in humans, McNaughton noted that the same sensor proteins are present in people and that studies with humans suggest that they behave in a similar way.

This research provides "valuable information" for understanding how the proteins responsible for sensing temperature work, Caterina said. Understanding these mechanisms could be useful for studying conditions like neuropathic pain, in which people's sensitivity to heat and cold is enhanced.

"What kinds of signals create our daily experiences around temperature is by itself very important," he told Live Science. "It's a big part of understanding ourselves as living beings."

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

#6433. Asteroid Mining Will Crash the Platinum Market, But That’s Good News for Earth

Science fiction authors have been dreaming of robotic spacecraft harvesting fortunes from asteroids for decades. Humanity is slowly getting closer to that reality. But if you ask asteroid mining skeptics, they will usually ask one specific question - what happens to the prices of all those rare materials once someone actually brings them back? A pair of system dynamicists from MIT directly tackled that question with a new paper titled Will AstroForge Collapse the PGM Market?

Platinum Group Metals, or PGMs, are absolutely critical to modern industry. Two of the most commonly used are platinum and palladium, which are critical components in everything from automotive catalytic converters (hence when thereâs a raft of people stealing them) to hydrogen fuel cells. However, these materials are exceptionally hard to come by - on Earth at least. More than 80% of the known planetary reserves are locked in deep-shaft mines located in South Africa and Russia.

Their absurd prices (tens of millions of dollars a ton) are based at least in part on how difficult they are to extract. Even at the Russian and South African mines, they are only able to glean a few grams of material per ton of rock. In the process, they require ventilation, cooling, and heavy machinery, as well as actual laborers down deep mine shafts. That sounds exactly like the kind of industry that is ripe for disruption - at least if there is another source of the raw material.

Fraser talks about whether we will mine asteroids.

Luckily, there is. Metallic (M-type) asteroids are the leftover metallic cores of protoplanets, and carry concentrations of PGMs dozens of times higher than even the richest mines on Earth. A single kilometer-wide space rock of this type holds more PGMs than humans have extracted throughout all recorded history. No wonder these particular materials have been the focus on asteroid mining efforts for decades.

AstroForge, a start-up based in California, is one of a second-round of asteroid mining start-ups that are focusing specifically on returning PGMs to Earthâs market. Instead of multi-billion dollar asteroid mining craft, they specialize in small, agile probes that cost only a few million dollars each to launch. The value of what they return, though, is much higher.

Their architecture involves latching on to the metallic asteroid using magnets. High power lasers then vaporize the asteroidâs crust, and an onboard refinery separates the PGM gas from the less valuable nickel and iron that makes up the majority of the asteroidâs bulk. After the PGMs have been refined, they are blasted back to Earth in a heat-shielded return capsule, ready to be brought to market on Earth itself. That way, the company only ships high value material rather than processing minerals that donât have as much value back down on Earth.

Isaac Arthur is much more bullish on our eventual ability to mine asteroids, as he discusses in this video. Credit - Isaac Arthur YouTube Channel

Understanding how this would affect the terrestrial market is the focus of the paper, and researchers Robert Nachtrieb and Steven Smith built a dynamic computer simulation tracking what they believe will happen to the PGM market over a 20 year period following the first successful return of a chunk of material from an asteroid. According to their model, there will be a dramatic, two-phase transition.

The first phase can be thought of as a âspace gold rushâ. The prices for PGMs have been held artificially high by lack of supply - a classic problem in traditional economics. Once the supplied amount changes - such as when new sources come online, the price begins to fall as the supply line of the classic âXâ graph moves to the right. But it doesnât happen overnight. At the start, space-based metals will be able to be sold at normal prices, allowing the asteroid mining companies to enjoy astronomical profit margins.

Those profit margins will, at least in theory, drive plenty of additional private investment, which in turn will be used to expand the production capacity of the space-based options. According to the paper, this will drive a cycle where industry profits will skyrocket to eight times what they currently are during this first phase. Thatâs enough to make whoever successfully send material back first fabulously wealthy.

But eventually, the second act will begin - what the authors describe as equilibrium collapse. Global supply of PGMs will far exceed original terrestrial amounts, and the market prices will start falling dramatically. High cost mines, such as those operating in North America, will be the first casualties. The Russian and South African behemoths, though, will not be far behind, as they will be unable to maintain a profit with the lower price caused by the increased supply. Over the course of fifteen years, terrestrial mining supplies will be completely replaced by space-mined ones, and market prices will drop by over 75%.

That might sound like terrible news for the terrestrial mining industry - and to put it bluntly, it is. But itâs great news for everyone else. Cheaper PGMs mean less expensive hydrogen electrolyzers, and therefore a less expensive transition to the âgreen economyâ for the rest of the world. In addition, space-based mining does not have all the acid mine drainage, arsenic pollution, and hazardous labor in deep tunnels that are required to get PGMs out of the ground on Earth.

Which all sounds like a much better future for humanity more generally. The problem is the engineering challenges to get to that point. Astroforge has had a few high-profile failures during its development cycle so far. But thatâs the case with any fast-moving ânew spaceâ company. It is undeniably getting closer to making this future world of green tech provided by space rocks a reality. And, if they do manage to do so, everyone involved should become extremely wealthy in a span of less than two decades.

#6432. Something Unusual Is Swirling around the Monster Black Hole at the Center of Our Galaxy

Webb’s measurements of metal-rich gas offer clues to the processes that fuel our galaxy’s supermassive black hole, which consumes material more slowly than others.

The gas circling the Milky Way’s central black hole is rich in metals, probably supplied by stars that exploded and released material into its surroundings over time. Researchers at McGill University’s Trottier Space Institute uncovered chemical enrichment around Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*), offering clues to the origins of the material available for the black hole to consume.

For astronomers, “metals” means every element heavier than hydrogen and helium. The category includes carbon and oxygen as well as iron and gold.

Sgr A* is closer to Earth than any other supermassive black hole, making it easier to observe. The team studied its surroundings using data from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), launched five years ago. The telescope measures infrared light across a wide range of wavelengths with unprecedented spectral and spatial resolution. Those capabilities allowed the researchers to distinguish the heat signatures of multiple gas clouds orbiting near the black hole and precisely measure each cloud’s metal composition.

The gas also turned out to have a composition similar to that of many stars orbiting Sgr A*. That resemblance suggests the gas and stars may have formed together. The researchers said the findings could help explain how metals are distributed around supermassive black holes in more distant galaxies, as well as the processes that supplied Earth with many of these elements.

Chemical composition also affects what happens to the gas. Metals influence how quickly it cools, which in turn influences how readily the black hole can draw it in.

“We know there’s a black hole at the center of our galaxy pulling material into itself, but we see that it’s eating a lot less material than other supermassive black holes, and more slowly,” said Nicole Ford, the study’s lead author and a PhD student in Professor Daryl Haggard’s research group in McGill’s Department of Physics. “Part of understanding why this is happening means looking at the properties of the materials available for it to consume, including gas, dust and the stars orbiting around it.”

The findings complement a recent study led by Banting Postdoctoral Fellow Mayura Balakrishnan, which examined whether the surrounding gas retained evidence of earlier bursts of energy from the black hole. That study found that local conditions shape the light emitted by the gas, making the black hole’s influence difficult to isolate. The results do not rule out past outbursts. They show that the surrounding gas cannot provide a reliable history of the black hole’s activity.

Ford said understanding how Sgr A* attracts material will require comparing these observations with simulations of how gas evolves over longer timescales.

References: “Ionization Structure and Metal Enrichment of the Galactic Center Minispiral Observed with JWST” by Nicole M. Ford, Mayura Balakrishnan, Sebastiano D. von Fellenberg, Daryl Haggard, Joseph M. Michail, Yuzhu Cui, Joseph L. Hora, Joey Neilsen, Giacomo Principe, Tamojeet Roychowdhury, Nadeen B. Sabha, Howard A. Smith, Zach Sumners and S. P. Willner, 19 October 2026, The Astronomical Journal. DOI: 10.3847/1538-3881/ae994d

“Isolating Sgr A East: The First Uncontaminated X-Ray Maps of a Galactic Center Supernova Remnant” by Mayura Balakrishnan, Adrien Picquenot, Lia Corrales, Q. Daniel Wang, Fabio Acero and Rodolfo Montez, 20 May 2026, The Astrophysical Journal. DOI: 10.3847/1538-4357/ae5dbe

#6430. A drug-free diabetes treatment? An implant lowers blood sugar in mice

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The device banishes extra blood glucose by converting it to a compound excreted in urine

Excess blood glucose (shown in white in this illustration) is the target of a new experimental device. In mice, the sugar gets converted into a compound which the kidneys can excrete in urine.

NEMES LASZLO/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

A wireless implant that clears excess sugar from the blood could someday offer a drug-free way to treat type 2 diabetes and obesity.

In mice with both conditions, the under-the-skin device brought high blood sugar back to normal within 60 to 90 minutes of being switched on, researchers report October 22 in Science. After six weeks, the treated mice lost up to 10 percent of their body weight and had lower triglycerides, a type of fat in the blood.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Diabetes affects about 830 million people worldwide. Conventional type 2 diabetes treatments like insulin and GLP-1 drugs require careful dosing. Even experimental diabetes-controlling implants still rely on the hormone insulin, which clears sugar from the bloodstream but doesn’t rid the body of it, says Martin Fussenegger, a bioengineer at ETH Zurich. The new implant instead removes glucose from the body without added drugs, genes or living cells.

The 3-centimeter-long device contains a catalyst made of gold flakes and platinum particles on spongelike graphite. When electricity powers it, the catalyst converts glucose into gluconate, a compound that is easier for the kidneys to flush out in urine. With less glucose available for energy, the body may turn to its fat stores instead, Fussenegger and colleagues suspect. In mice, that shift showed up as higher blood levels of chemicals released when fat breaks down, such as ketones. “This system kind of targets the root cause, which is the energy surplus by glucose in the body,” Fussenegger says.

The implant works like an automatic sugar-removal system: A wearable glucose monitor detects high blood sugar levels and sends readings through a smartphone that switches the implant on. When levels return to a safer range, it switches off. The automated system ran for two weeks in eight mice. The catalyst itself remained able to convert glucose after up to three months under their skin, though the study didn’t establish how long the entire device would last.

And it’s still unknown how well the device would work in people. “This is a potentially promising method,” says David Klonoff, an endocrinologist at Sutter Mills-Peninsula Medical Center in Burlingame, Calif., who was not involved in the study. “But the risks are significant and must be carefully ruled out before it can be safely tested on humans.”

Researchers need to determine how much gluconate the kidneys can clear, Klonoff says. If it builds up, it could disrupt the body’s acid-base balance, causing symptoms such as nausea or confusion; excreting it could also deplete electrolytes such as sodium and potassium, he notes.

Scaling up the device is another challenge. Humans consume about 250 grams of carbohydrates daily, compared with two grams for mice, Klonoff estimates. Meeting that demand could require a much larger implant or multiple devices, he says. In a lab test, a larger device cleared nearly all glucose from about 5 liters of solution, roughly an adult’s blood volume, though not a full day’s glucose intake.

Fussenegger’s team plans to test the device in pigs and sheep before considering human trials. If proven safe and effective, it could offer an alternative to existing diabetes treatments and a new weight-loss option for people regardless of whether they have diabetes, he says.

#6429. James Webb Discovers a Nearly Pristine Galaxy From the Dawn of the Universe

JWST image of the massive galaxy cluster MACS J0416 (background) and a three-color composite of the extremely faint galaxy LAP1-B (inset). Invisible in the NIRCam image, LAP1-B was detected through sensitive NIRSpec observations of hydrogen and oxygen emissions. The inset shows gas velocity and spatial distribution (blue: hydrogen Lyα; green: oxygen [OIII]; red: hydrogen Hα), with Lyα shifted by 200 km/s for clarity. Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA & K. Nakajima et al., Nature.A galaxy seen 13 billion years ago has just 1/240th the Sun’s oxygen abundance, offering a rare glimpse of what the ancestors of the Milky Way’s faintest neighbors may have looked like.

Some of the faintest galaxies near the Milky Way may be survivors from the earliest chapters of cosmic history. Their ancient stars preserve clues about how galaxies formed, but astronomers have struggled to connect these nearby relics to the small, primitive galaxies that existed billions of years ago.

An international research team led by Associate Professor Kimihiko Nakajima of Kanazawa University has now identified a possible link. A tiny galaxy called LAP1-B, seen as it existed 13 billion years ago, contains remarkably little oxygen and has several characteristics that resemble some of the oldest galaxies still found near the Milky Way.

The chemical evidence reaches back to a time when the universe was only beginning to acquire the elements familiar to us today. Shortly after the Big Bang, the universe consisted primarily of hydrogen and helium. Heavier elements, including the carbon and oxygen essential for life, were produced later inside the first generations of stars and eventually released into space.

Astronomers have long wanted to study galaxies from this early period to understand how those elements first accumulated. The challenge is that such galaxies are extraordinarily small and faint, making their chemical composition difficult to measure even with powerful telescopes.

LAP1-B became accessible thanks to gravitational lensing, a phenomenon in which the gravity of a massive object bends and magnifies light from something farther away. In this case, a massive galaxy cluster amplified the distant galaxy’s light approximately 100 times, allowing researchers to examine an object that would otherwise be extremely difficult to study.

Building on earlier detections, the team observed LAP1-B for more than 30 hours using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). They used spectroscopy, a technique that analyzes light to identify the chemical elements present in a distant object.

The observations revealed an oxygen abundance just 1/240th that of the Sun, a record low that places LAP1-B among the most chemically primitive galaxies ever characterized.

“I was instantly thrilled by the extreme lack of oxygen revealed in the data,” says Associate Professor Nakajima, the research team leader. “Finding a galaxy in such a primitive state is astonishing. It’s a chemical signature that clearly indicates a primordial galaxy caught in the moments shortly after its formation.”

The researchers also found an unusually high ratio of carbon to oxygen. That distinction matters because the relative amounts of different elements can reveal how a galaxy acquired its chemical ingredients. In LAP1-B, the elevated carbon-to-oxygen ratio closely matches theoretical predictions for material scattered into space by the explosions of the universe’s first-generation stars.

Together, these measurements suggest that LAP1-B was observed during an exceptionally early stage of chemical enrichment, when the products of the first stars were beginning to accumulate in its gas.

“Usually, we act like ‘cosmic archaeologists,’ trying to guess the past by looking at old stars in our own neighborhood. But now, we can analyze the gas directly from the original scene 13 billion years ago,” emphasizes Nakajima. “We are witnessing the moment when a galaxy first inherited the chemical building blocks created by the universe’s earliest stars.”

The galaxy’s extremely small size provides another clue about its origins. The team estimates that LAP1-B contains less than 3,300 times the Sun’s mass in stars and is associated with a halo dominated by dark matter, the invisible material thought to account for much of the mass in galaxies.

Those characteristics resemble a class of nearby objects called ultra-faint dwarf galaxies (UFDs). These exceptionally dim galaxies contain ancient stars and relatively few heavy elements, leading astronomers to suspect that they preserve conditions from the universe’s earliest periods of galaxy formation.

“UFDs are not only the faintest galaxies; they are composed of ancient stars over 12 billion years old and are often described as ‘fossils of the universe,'” explains Professor Masami Ouchi (NAOJ/University of Tokyo), a member of the research team. “Astronomers suspected they might be the remains of the universe’s earliest galaxies because they lack heavy elements, but astronomers never had a direct link—until we found LAP1-B.”

LAP1-B offers a rare opportunity to examine what a possible predecessor of these nearby galaxies actually looked like billions of years ago. Its low oxygen abundance, unusual carbon-to-oxygen ratio, and dark matter-dominated structure are consistent with the idea that today’s ultra-faint dwarf galaxies descended from small systems that formed very early in cosmic history.

“It is a profound surprise to find that LAP1-B looks exactly like the ‘ancestor’ we had only imagined in theories. This helps us solve the mystery of why these cosmic fossils have survived in their current form to the present day.”

Although the findings provide a compelling connection between early galaxies and nearby cosmic fossils, LAP1-B represents one example. Examining more objects with similarly primitive chemical compositions could help researchers determine how common these early systems were and how they developed into the galaxies observed today.

The team plans to continue using JWST to search for even more chemically primitive galaxies, with the ultimate goal of identifying some of the first galaxies ever formed. Such observations could help establish when the earliest stars began producing heavier elements and how those materials spread through the young universe.

Associate Professor Nakajima concludes, “We hope this discovery marks a historic step in understanding how the elements that make up our own bodies were first born and accumulated across the Universe.”

Reference: “An ultra-faint, chemically primitive galaxy forming in the reionization era” by Kimihiko Nakajima, Masami Ouchi, Yuichi Harikane, Eros Vanzella, Yoshiaki Ono, Yuki Isobe, Moka Nishigaki, Takuji Tsujimoto, Fumitaka Nakamura, Yi Xu, Hiroya Umeda and Yechi Zhang, 13 May 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-10374-1

This research was supported by the following organizations and grants: Japan Society for the Promotion of Science (JSPS): KAKENHI Grants (No. JP20K22373, JP24K07102, JP20H00180, JP21H04467, JP25H00674, JP24H00245, JP24KJ0202, JP23H00132) Japan Science and Technology Agency (JST): Grant JPMJFS2136 National Institute for Astrophysics (INAF): GO Grants 2022 (“The revolution is around the corner: JWST will probe globular cluster precursors and Population III stellar clusters at cosmic dawn”) and 2024 (“Mapping Star Cluster Feedback in a Galaxy 450 Myr after the Big Bang”) European Union: NextGenerationEU (PRIN 2022 project n.20229YBSAN)

#6428. The Ice Giants' Magnetic Fields are Very Strange Compared to Earth's

Most planets appear to have magnetic fields, even if they're only weak, remnant fields. Earth has a strong field generated by its internal geodynamo. The other rocky planets have magnetic fields of varying strengths, with the possible exception of Venus. The outer gas planets, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune, all have strong dynamos.

But the magnetic fields generated by the ice giants Uranus and Neptune have some strange properties.

Earth's molten core and internal convection generate its magnetic fields. But the ice giants' magnetic fields are likely generated by fluids that are electrically conductive. These are water, ammonia, and methane ices under extreme pressure and temperatures that alter them and turn them into ionic and superionic phases. Not only is their electrical conductivity at play, but so is convection and the planets' rotations.

But beyond what generates them, they also have other differences. Earth's magnetic field has well-defined north and south poles that drift a little over time, and even flip every couple of hundred thousand years or so. But Voyager 2 showed us how different Uranus and Neptune are. Their fields are in disarray compared to Earth's. They're tilted and multi-peaked.

Uranus' magnetic field doesn't originate in its center, and is tilted almost 60 degrees from its axis of rotation. It's overall geometry is strange, and the magnetic field across its surface is asymmetrical in strength.

Neptune's magnetic field is similarly strange, but weaker. Like Uranus' it's tilted from its rotational axis, by about 47 degrees. It's also offset from the planet's physical center like Uranus'.

The most critical difference between the magnetic fields of Earth and those of Uranus and Neptune is that the fields around the ice giants experience shorter-term variability. In short, they're a weird mess.

While planetary scientists know that these fields are generated inside the planets, they've had to make some guesses as to why they're so strange. New research in Nature Communications Physics has made some progress understanding the pair of ice giants and their strange magnetic fields. It's titled "Electrical conductivity structure drives anomalous and potentially time-varying magnetic fields at Uranus and Neptune," and the lead author is Chi Yan. Yan is a research associate at the University of Texax Jackson School of Geosciences.

"Uranus and Neptune exhibit magnetic fields that are non-dipolar and non-axisymmetric, unlike those of any other known planet," the researchers write. "These fields are generated by fluid motions in electrically conducting planetary interiors via dynamo action, offering a window into otherwise inaccessible deep processes."

As we often say at Universe Today, understanding the oddballs and outliers in a group of objects sheds light on how processes operate across the broader group they're a part of. This is true of the ice giants and their magnetic fields. "Understanding why Uranus and Neptune have such unusual magnetic fields provides critical insight into dynamo processes across planets and stars," the authors explain.

This work is based on modelled dynamos that are controlled by interior composition and temperature. They assumed that electrical conductivity increases with depth. The authors say they "produce large-scale magnetic features consistent with the observed fields of Uranus and Neptune..."

This schematic shows the different interior layouts used in the models. a through c show radially variable electrical conductivity profiles for dynamo models with convective shell geometries. d through f show the associated shell geometry for each of a through c. Image Credit: Yan, C., Soderlund, K.M., Aurnou, J.M. et al. Electrical conductivity structure drives anomalous and potentially time-varying magnetic fields at Uranus and Neptune. Commun Phys 9, 336 (2026).

âDeep inside Uranus and Neptune, pressures and temperatures become extremely high,â lead author Yan said in a press release. âUnder these conditions, which can cause water molecules to break apart into ions, the material may become increasingly electrically conductive with depth.â

Voyager 2 gave us our only good close-up look at Uranus and Neptune. It likely caught those fields in a snapshot in time, and the model shows both planets' magnetic fields could shift and change markedly in only decades. The fields are most likely configured much differently than when Voyager 2 visited. This is much different than on Earth, where the magnetic north pole drifts between about 5 and 60 km per year, or about one degree every few decades.

"These non-dipolar dynamos exhibit substantial temporal variation, although the rate fluctuates and can be transiently slow," the authors write. They explain that changes in both intensity and orientation are a possibility in the decades since Voyager 2 flew past Uranus and Neptune, "though the extent of any such variation remains poorly constrained observationally as each planet has been measured in situ only once."

âEarthâs magnetic tilt drifts by only a degree or so over 50 years,â said Yan. âOur models show the ice giants can behave very differently. In some stretches the tilt swings by tens of degrees within decades. In others it shifts only slightly over the same span.â

This figure compares observations of Uranus' and Neptune's surface magnetic fields with the fields from models. The figure "demonstrates that the most Uranus-like snapshot from Model 6 (panel c) and the most Neptune-like snapshot from Model 11 (panel d) can change substantially on decadal timescales, with their close morphological resemblance to the respective observed fields (panels a and b) deteriorating markedly after 32 years (panels e and f)," the authors explain. Image Credit: Yan, C., Soderlund, K.M., Aurnou, J.M. et al. Electrical conductivity structure drives anomalous and potentially time-varying magnetic fields at Uranus and Neptune. Commun Phys 9, 336 (2026).

"We demonstrate that dynamo models incorporating an electrical conductivity that increases with depth can promote non-dipolar, non-axisymmetric magnetic fields," the authors write, including the M1 peak observed at Uranus and Neptune.

The M1 peak is an important, maybe the most important part, of Voyager 2's magnetic field observations. M=1 represents the lop-sided parts of a magnetic field. On Earth and other planets like Jupiter and Saturn, the magnetic field's power is dominated by symmetric or M=0 components. So for those planets, the M-1 components are at least an order of magnitude weaker than their M-0 components.

But that's not true on Uranus and Neptune. They show a stark contrast. They both have a very strong M-1 peak, the part that represents asymmetric fields. This means that they have dipoles, quadrupoles, and octupoles that are messy and skewed from the axis of rotation.

"Despite current observational and computational limitations, our results indicate that ice-giant-like dynamos can, in some intervals, undergo substantial magnetic field variations on decadal timescales that, if confirmed by future in situ or auroral measurements, could have significant impacts on the surrounding planetary magnetospheres," the authors write.

The JWST has observed the ice giant aurorae and the charged particles involved. These particles respond to the magnetic fields, and those observations could confirm if the magnetic fields have indeed shifted since Voyager 2 visited. Researchers are still working on those observations.

The image on the left is an enhanced-color image of Neptune from NASAâs Hubble Space Telescope. On the right, that image is combined with data from NASAâs James Webb Space Telescope. The cyan splotches are auroral activity captured with the JWST's Near-Infrared Spectrograph (NIRSpec). Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Heidi Hammel (AURA), Henrik Melin (Northumbria University), Leigh Fletcher (University of Leicester), Stefanie Milam (NASA-GSFC)

âWe are busy working on whatâs contained within these observations, but the shape and structure of the aurora, as well as other weird patterns in the ionosphere promises to provide us with a way of understanding how the magnetic fields have changed, an important stepping stone,â said Tom Stallard, a professor at Northumbria University who led the JWST observation campaign.

The researchers will combine the JWST data with their models and data from Voyager 2 and take their results as far as they can to try to determine the state of the magnetic fields today. But they're up against some limitations, limitations that can only be lifted by another mission to the ice giants.

There are no firm plans for a mission to the ice giants, but there are concepts. One is NASA's Uranus Orbiter & Probe that would study the planet and its moons, and even send a probe into Uranus' atmosphere. The Neptune Odyssey is another NASA concept. It would also consist of an orbiter and an atmospheric probe. The science community has recognized the importance of these missions, but they're just concepts at this point.

This research may extend to the issue of habitability, though probably only tangentially. Uranus' four major moons could all potentially have subsurface oceans under icy covers, though this is far from confirmed. If they do, then Uranus' magnetic field and related radiation belts could affect these bodies of water, their longevity, and their potential habitability.

#6427. An Ancient Virus May Hold the Secret to What Makes the Human Brain Different

Could a virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago help explain how the human brain became different?

Researchers at Lund University have discovered that ancient viral DNA embedded in the chimpanzee genome silences a gene involved in early human brain development. Their study, published in Science Advances, found that the gene, LINC00662, remains active in human brain organoids, where it helps support the development of nerve cells and the connections between them.

The finding offers a way to explore how humans and chimpanzees developed different biological traits despite sharing much of their genetic makeup. Evolution can change how existing genes are used, as well as which genes a species carries.

“The virus we investigated specifically affected chimpanzees. Yet humans and chimpanzees have largely the same genetic makeup. That is why it is important to understand the differences in how genes are regulated. Our findings suggest that one gene, LINC00662, plays a significant role in early human brain development,” says Johan Jakobsson, professor of molecular neurogenetics at Lund University.

The genetic remnant belongs to PTERV1, an endogenous retrovirus. Its DNA became embedded in the chimpanzee genome during an ancient infection and has been inherited ever since. The researchers found copies of the viral sequence at numerous locations throughout chimpanzee DNA.

Those sequences are systematically shut down through methylation, a chemical process that helps regulate gene activity. At the LINC00662 location, the inherited viral insertion also keeps the neighboring gene silent.

To examine this difference during brain development, the team grew brain organoids from human and chimpanzee stem cells. These miniature, three-dimensional structures resemble brain tissue and reproduce some features of its early development.

“The gene was strongly expressed in the human organoids, but not at all in the chimpanzee organoids,” says Patricia Gerdes, a postdoctoral researcher in molecular neurogenetics at Lund University.

The researchers then tested whether the viral sequence caused the shutdown. Using the CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing tool, they removed it from chimpanzee cells. LINC00662 became active again.

“This shows that it is in fact the viral insertion that is responsible for the gene being switched off in chimpanzees,” says Patricia Gerdes.

A separate experiment explored the gene’s role in humans. When the team used CRISPR to silence LINC00662 in human brain organoids, genes involved in nerve cell development and the formation of connections between those cells became less active.

For Jakobsson, the results show how an infection can leave a lasting genetic change across a population, while helping explain how gene regulation can protect the brain or contribute to damage. The team will next investigate whether other viral remnants influenced brain evolution and whether such sequences are linked to brain diseases.

Reference: “Retroviral insertions contributed to the divergence of human and chimpanzee brains” by Patricia Gerdes, Ofelia Karlsson, Raquel Garza, Diahann A. M. Atacho, PingHsun Hsieh, Bharat Prajapati, DongAhn Yoo, Chandramouli Muralidharan, Anita Adami, Carrie Davis-Hansson, Emily M. Johansson, Yogita Sharma, Laura Castilla-Vallmanya, Wiktor West, Meghna Vinod, Lucian Domitrovic, Pia A. Johansson, Jenny Johansson, Christopher H. Douse, Chandrasekhar Kanduri, Patric Jern, Evan E. Eichler and Johan Jakobsson, 23 October 2026, Science Advances. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeg5791

This study was funded by the Swedish Research Council; the Swedish Brain Foundation; Cancerfonden; Barncancerfonden; the Swedish Government Initiative for Strategic Research Areas (MultiPark & StemTherapy); and the European Union’s Horizon Europe research and innovation program.

A double subduction zone off the coast of Japan caused rifting halfway around the world to accelerate, fueling the formation of some of North America's most iconic features.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A geological reorganization near Japan may have led to the formation of one of North America's most recognizable features.

The birth of the Gulf of California, which rifted from Mexico and created the Baja Peninsula 6 million to 8 million years ago, was accelerated by the formation of a double subduction zone more than 6,000 miles (9,600 kilometers) away, near Japan. This reorganization led to a transfer of tectonic force across the Pacific tectonic plate, which, in turn, opened the Gulf of California and ultimately led to the Grand Canyon's formation, according to new research published Oct. 29 in the journal Science.

The findings will help researchers understand more about plate boundaries, which is where most of the strongest earthquakes on the planet originate.

"It's more than a regional curiosity," study co-author Thorsten Becker, a geophysicist at the University of Texas at Austin (UT Austin), told Live Science. "It's a reminder of the global connectedness of mantle convection and plate tectonics."

The Gulf of California is an example of a rift zone, a place where continental crust pulls apart and creates a spot so low that it can be filled by ocean water. There are many rift zones around the world; a currently active one is the Red Sea. But rifting can slow down, speed up or peter out entirely. In the Gulf of California, rifting not only persisted, but sped up. Rifting took about 6 million to 13 million years ‪—‬ much quicker than the typical speed of 30 million to 80 million years.

Study co-author Guido Gianni, a geophysicist at the Czech Academy of Sciences, wondered why that was. No previous research fully explained the rapid rifting, which changed the face of North America in many ways. Not only did the rifting transfer Baja California to the Pacific Plate, but it provided an outlet for the developing Colorado River, which subsequently carved the Grand Canyon on its way to sea level.

Gianni and Becker's doctoral student at UT Austin, Xiang He, used a global model of plate tectonics, run on supercomputers at the Texas Advanced Computing Center on campus, to find out if far-flung forces might provide an explanation. Around the same time the Gulf of California was pulling apart, Japan was undergoing its own geological changes. Off the coast of Japan, the Pacific Plate subducts, or pushes under, the Eurasian Plate. About 10 million to 12 million years ago, a single subduction zone near Japan transitioned into two separate subduction zones.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

A double subduction zone off Japan (left inset) accelerated the growth of the Gulf of California (right inset).

This transition at the western end of the Pacific Plate influenced the tectonic forces on the other side of the plate, He, Gianni, Becker and their colleagues found.

"It turned out — ta-da! — [with] the change in this pulling stress, Baja California was one of the few places outside the Japan region that were affected," Becker said. It was "unexpected and sort of a little bit too good to be true."

The researchers tweaked their model to see if the result held with different assumptions about stresses and mantle properties, and it did.

The Gulf of California was already rifting regardless of the situation across the Pacific. The initial rift was caused by the subduction of a tectonic plate called the Farallon Plate, located under the West Coast of North America. The Farallon slab stretched and thinned the continental crust of the North American plate as it moved. But such rifting might have ended with nothing more than the formation of a little valley or low spot if Japan's influence had not kicked in to give the rifting some extra oomph.

The findings have a direct effect on scientists' understanding of how plate boundaries form, Becker said. And this isn't just academic. The findings could have implications for understanding earthquake-generating faults such as the San Andreas in California and the Cascadia subduction zone in the Pacific Northwest, Becker said. Cascadia is what's known as a "megathrust" boundary, capable of triggering quakes of more than magnitude 9.

"If I'm asking what is the mantle doing underneath Cascadia so I get our megathrust correct," Becker said, "I need to include these effects."

Gianni, G. M., He, X., Becker, T. W., & Faccenna, C. (2026). Western Pacific double subduction drives Gulf of California rifting. Science, 394(6823), 515–519. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aef5187

Stephanie Pappas is a contributing writer for Live Science, covering topics ranging from geoscience to archaeology to the human brain and behavior. She was previously a senior writer for Live Science but is now a freelancer based in Denver, Colorado, and regularly contributes to Scientific American and The Monitor, the monthly magazine of the American Psychological Association. Stephanie received a bachelor's degree in psychology from the University of South Carolina and a graduate certificate in science communication from the University of California, Santa Cruz.
